title: Event Consumer Overload: Who Sets the Delivery Pace

steps.prompt: An external Java service subscribes to order platform events with a CometD client. During sales peaks that last up to two hours, events arrive faster than the service can process them, and its in-memory queue overflows and drops events. Which subscription design should the architect choose?

options.label: Subscribe through Pub/Sub API and request each next batch of events after finishing one
options.rationale: Pub/Sub API is the recommended path for external event streams, and its subscriptions are pull-based: the client asks for a set number of events, while CometD long polling hands over whatever the server has. Pulling at its own pace lets the service ride out a two-hour peak, with unread events held on the bus for up to 72 hours.

options.label: Keep the CometD client and enlarge its in-memory queue to hold a full sales peak
options.rationale: A bigger queue only delays the overflow: CometD still delivers at the server’s pace, so a two-hour peak keeps filling memory faster than the service drains it.

options.label: Run several CometD client instances subscribed to the same channel to share the load
options.rationale: Each CometD subscriber on a channel receives every event, so extra instances multiply the work and create duplicate processing instead of splitting the stream.

options.label: Have Salesforce send each order as an Outbound Message to a SOAP endpoint on the service
options.rationale: Outbound Messaging is a legacy SOAP push channel, so the service still receives messages at Salesforce’s pace and gains no control over the delivery rate.
